old: renowned among mankind for all manner of subtlety
reason: "Subtlety" as a noun meaning craftiness/cunning is an unusual, dated usage for a listener; today the word almost always means delicacy or nuance, so a first-time listener may momentarily misread Odysseus's self-description.

old: toward the time when men unyoke their oxen
reason: A period farming reference used purely as a time marker; a modern listener has to infer "end of the workday/evening" from an unfamiliar agricultural image rather than being told directly.

old: for sportsmen—who as a rule will suffer so much hardship in forest or among mountain precipices—do not go there
new: for even sportsmen, who will normally put up with great hardship in forests or on mountain cliffs, do not bother to go there
reason: Inverted causal syntax ("for sportsmen ... do not go there" with the reason for the goats' safety buried in a long parenthetical aside) is hard to parse by ear on first hearing.

old: Thus through the livelong day to the going down of the sun we ate and drank our fill
new: So all through the day, until the sun went down, we ate and drank our fill
reason: "Livelong day" is archaic poetic diction a general listener won't use or immediately recognize; meaning is guessable from context but adds friction.
"Hawsers" is a specialized nautical term unfamiliar to most general listeners; the action (untying the ship to leave) is inferable but the word itself is a stumble.

old: It was a station for a great many sheep and goats
new: It was a shelter for a great many sheep and goats
reason: "Station" used to mean an animal pen/shelter is a dated sense of the word; a contemporary listener's first association (transit station) briefly misdirects the image.

old: We drove the sharp end of the beam into the monster’s eye, and bearing on it with all my weight I kept turning it round and round as though I were boring a hole in a ship’s plank with an auger, which two men with a wheel and strap can keep on turning as long as they choose.
new: We drove the sharp end of the beam into the monster's eye and, bearing on it with all my weight, kept turning it round and round. It was like boring a hole in a ship's plank with an auger, the kind two men can keep turning with a strap and wheel for as long as they like.
reason: One long sentence stacks the main action, a participial clause, a simile, and a trailing relative clause ("which two men with a wheel and strap can keep on turning") that refers back several clauses to "an auger." Heard aloud, a listener is likely to lose track of what "which" refers to before the sentence resolves.

old: even so did the Cyclops’ eye hiss round the beam of olive wood
new: in just the same way the Cyclops’ eye hissed around the beam of olive wood
reason: The "As a blacksmith ... even so did..." correlative construction is period syntax; "even so" meaning "likewise/just so" is not how a modern listener parses the phrase on first hearing (it more readily reads as a concessive "nevertheless").
"Gobbets" is an uncommon, archaic word for a general listener; meaning is recoverable from context but is an unnecessary vocabulary hurdle in an already intense sentence.

old: Thus through the livelong day to the going down of the sun we feasted our fill on meat and drink
new: So all through the day, until the sun went down, we feasted our fill on meat and drink
reason: Second occurrence of the same archaic "livelong day" formula (see paragraph 8); consistent with itself but the phrase itself remains a stumbling point for a general listener each time it recurs.
